en: *Mahāyāna-pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra*, one fascicle. Composed by the Noble Ureṇaka.

Translated by [the monk] who holds the rank of Kaifu Yitong Sanci, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Duke of Sushan with a fief of three thousand households, conferred the purple robe, and posthumously titled司空 (Sikong).
From one arises three; from three, six are produced.
From six and two, again six arise; from six, further six are born.
From six there are three; these three, in turn, have three more.
The three again give rise to the four, and the four again give rise to the three.
From the three they arise as one, and that one again gives rise to seven.
Whatever suffering exists therein, the Muni has declared it all to be subsumed.
The wise declare that these twelvefold distinctions are empty;
through the power of dependent origination, one should understand these twelve factors.
Ignorance, karma, and consciousness, as well as name-and-form, the sense faculties, and the triad of contact—
Appropriation, thirst, and grasping; Accumulation, birth, and the sequence ending with decay.
The first, eighth, and ninth are afflictions (*kleśa*); The second and tenth are karma;
The remaining seven are all suffering (*duḥkha*). These three categories encompass the twelve factors.
The first two belong to the past, the latter two to the future time, and the remaining eight are of the present;
this is called the Dharma of the Three Times.
Afflictions and karma bring about retribution, and that retribution in turn gives rise to afflictions.
Afflictions give rise to karma, and from karma there is also retribution.
If one is free from affliction, how can there be karma?
If one is free from karma, how can there be retribution?
Without retribution, there is freedom from affliction; these three are each individually extinguished.
Five factors arise as causes producing effects, which are termed afflictions and karma;
seven factors constitute the effects, and these seven kinds of suffering should be known.
Within the cause there is no fruit, and within the fruit there is also no cause;
within the cause there is no cause, and within the fruit there is no fruit;
the wise one accords with emptiness.
Because cause and effect are conjoined, they exist; since afflictions, karma, and their fruits are conjoined, one should admit that there are six divisions.
There are two sections and three summaries; the intermingling of cause and effect constitutes the sections.
The summary of the third and fourth sections:
In the state of suffering there are five factors: the agent, the storehouse-consciousness, the objective realm, transformation, and the flow of existence.
The outflowing fruit (niṣyanda-phala) is twofold; within the factors of association and faculties, each is divided into three and two parts respectively.
From the transformation of the outflowing fruit, it arises within the remaining factors of association.
The one hundred and eleven dharmas arise through dependent origination by way of their conjunction; there is no sentient being and no life-principle—
this emptiness is that which wisdom knows.
Within non-self and that which is devoid of self, there is the emptiness of the four kinds of ignorance;
the remaining factors are likewise so. Free from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism—this is precisely the Middle Way.
The essence of awakening is the Buddhas; having awakened, among the assembly, the Sage Seer spoke of non-self.
The Teacher explained this meaning in the Kātyāyana Sūtra.
Right view and the view of emptiness—the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* (the name of which is associated with the lunar mansion Viśākhā)—also speak of supreme emptiness.
One who knows this corresponds to emptiness; yet, if one does not understand dependent origination, [one will not realize it].
Nor do they know that emptiness;
they feel no revulsion toward the aggregates. This is called the "emptiness of the miserable realms," for they are thus deluded regarding the meaning of dependent origination.
Free from pride, they know emptiness; because they have grown weary of the aggregates, they are not deluded regarding karma and its results.
Nor is it that they do not take this as an object; for when there is an object of emptiness, this [result] must exist.
The objects of experience resulting from karmic retribution have already been explained as dependent origination;
those afflictions, karma, and suffering are subsumed within these three categories according to the Dharma: from the three, the two arise.
From two arise seven; from seven, again, three arise.
Thus the wheel of existence turns; all things are cause and effect.
From emptiness arises emptiness; from phenomena arise phenomena.
Dependent on conditions, afflictions arise; Dependent on conditions, karma also arises;
Dependent on conditions, retribution also arises; There is not one thing that does not have conditions.
Recitation, lamps, seals, mirrors, and sound, Sunlight, seeds, and vinegar.
The continuity of the aggregates does not shift for even a moment; wisdom contemplates those two.
This concludes the root text of the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti-kārikā*.
I shall now provide an explanatory commentary on the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti-kārikā* in accordance with its sequential order.
From one arises three; from three, six are produced;
from six and two, again six; and from six, six are likewise produced.
That which arises as three from one refers to ignorance (*ajñāna*); this ignorance is termed *avidyā*.

Because one does not realize suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, it is called ignorance (*ajñāna*). Due to this ignorance, there arise meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable [karmas], which are termed the three types of formations (*trividhāḥ saṃskārāḥ*).
Furthermore, bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations arise from that transformation.

Regarding the six arising from the three: from the three types of formations, the six groups of consciousness arise, namely: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
"Six from two" means that those six groups of consciousness arise from two things, namely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

"Two from six" means that from the two types of name-and-form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise, namely: the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.
"From six, six also arise" means that from those six sense bases, six types of contact are produced: namely, eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.
From the six [bases] there arise the three; from these three, again, there are three;
from the three, four are produced; and from the four, three are produced again.

Regarding "from the six there arise the three": from those six contacts, the three feelings are subsequently produced—namely, pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

Regarding the statement that "these three further have three," it means that from those same three types of sensation, three kinds of craving arise in turn: namely, craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*), and craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).

Regarding "from three, one further gives rise to four": from those three types of craving, the four types of grasping arise, namely: grasping at sensory desire (*kāma-upādāna*), grasping at views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*), grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-upādāna*), and grasping at the doctrine of self (*ātman-vāda-upādāna*).
From the four, three are further produced; from those four graspings, the three realms of existence—namely, the existence of desire, the existence of form, and the formless existence—are generated.
From the three, one is produced; from that one, seven are further produced.
All the suffering contained therein is said by the Muni to be fully encompassed.
Regarding "from three, one arises": by taking those same three existences (*bhava*) as conditions, one type of future birth (*jāti*) arises.

Regarding "that one further gives rise to seven": from that single future existence (*bhava*), there further arise the seven kinds—namely, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.

Regarding the statement that "all suffering whatsoever is subsumed therein as taught by the Muni": herein, beginning with ignorance and ending with suffering, all the immeasurable varieties of suffering have been briefly explained by the Blessed One as being subsumed within this.
The wise declare that these twelve distinctions are empty;
because of the power of dependent origination, one should know these twelve factors.

Regarding "the wise declare that these twelve distinctions are empty": these twelve branches, such as ignorance and the rest, are all empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); one should understand that what has been thus described is merely emptiness.
Dharmas arise from emptiness, and emptiness arises from dharmas, because dharmas are produced by way of the factors of dependent origination.
One should know that regarding these twelve dharmas, they are to be understood in this manner through the power of their sequential arising.

Among those, the characteristic of delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*); the characteristic of the accumulation of the factors of existence (*saṃskāra*) at the stage of the phrase "those formations" is volitional formations;
the characteristic of the emergence of the subsequent link of rebirth at the stage of the phrase "consciousness" is consciousness (*vijñāna*);

the characteristic of the conjunction of the mental body and the physical body at the stage of the phrase "name-and-form" is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); [the characteristic of] the establishment at the stage of the phrase "the six sense bases" is...

The characteristic of the faculties is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The characteristic of the coming together of eye, form, and visual consciousness at the locus of the phrase "contact" is contact (*sparśa*).
The characteristic of the experience of the pleasant, the unpleasant, and the perverted at the locus of the phrase "feeling" is feeling (*vedanā*).

The characteristic of insatiability at the locus of the phrase "craving" is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). The characteristic of grasping and seizing at the locus of the phrase "clinging" is clinging (*upādāna*).
That which is the locus of the term "grasping" (upādāna) and is characterized by the body of name-and-form (nāmarūpakāya) is existence (bhava);

that which is the locus of the term "arising" (jāti) and is characterized by the origination of the aggregates (skandha-samudaya) is birth; that which is the locus of the term "aging" (jarā) and is characterized by maturation is aging;

that which is the locus of the term "death" (maraṇa) and is the severance of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is death; and that which is the locus of the term "sorrow" (śoka) and is characterized by agitation is sorrow.

That which is characterized by the sound of weeping at the place of the "sighing" phrase is sighing; that which is characterized by bodily affliction at the place of the "suffering" phrase is suffering;
that which is characterized by mental affliction at the place of the "grief" phrase is grief;
and that which is characterized by the aspect of harm at the place of the "feverish distress" phrases is distress.
Ignorance, karma, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, the threefold contact, sensation, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, maturation, and the final limit.

Among these, "ignorance" refers to *avidyā*; "karma" refers to *saṃskāra*; "consciousness" refers to *vijñāna*; "name-and-form" refers to the aggregate of the five *skandhas*; "the sense bases" refers to the *āyatana*s; "threefold contact" refers to *sparśa*; "sensation" refers to *vedanā*; "craving" refers to *tṛṣṇā*; "grasping" refers to *upādāna*; "becoming" refers to *bhava*; "birth" refers to *jāti*; "maturation" refers to *jarā*; and "the final limit" refers to *maraṇa*.
Furthermore, I shall explain in due order how these various characteristics are subsumed.
Among them, regarding the distinctions between afflictions and karma:
the first, eighth, and ninth are afflictions; the second and tenth are karma.
The remaining seven are all suffering; these three encompass the twelve factors.
The three afflictions are ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
The two karmas are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*).
The seven results are consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death.
These twelve factors are subsumed within three categories.
Furthermore, regarding the distinction of time:
the first two belong to the past, the latter two to the future, and the remaining eight to the present;
these are called the dharmas of the three times.

When ignorance and formations—the first two types—are in the past, birth and old age and death—the latter two types—are in the future; and consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, and becoming—these eight types—are in the present.
Furthermore, each of these arises in succession:
afflictions give rise to karma, which brings about retribution; retribution in turn gives rise to afflictions, and afflictions again give rise to karma;
likewise, it is through karma that there is retribution.
The three types—afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and retribution (*vipāka*)—are as previously described.
Due to those afflictions there is karma; due to karma there is retribution; and again, due to retribution there are afflictions. From afflictions there is karma, and from karma there is retribution.
Question:
By what is it meant that the afflictions are exhausted and each is individually stilled? Answer:
Apart from affliction, what karma could there be?
Apart from karma, what retribution could there be?
Without retribution, one is free from affliction; these three are each utterly quiescent.

If this mind is free from the defilement of afflictions, one does not accumulate karma; if one does not perform karma, one does not undergo retribution; and if retribution is extinguished, afflictions do not arise either. In this way, these three are each individually quiescent.
Furthermore, these possess the divisions of cause and effect:
the five factors that produce the fruit from the cause are termed afflictions and karma;
the seven factors are taken as the fruit, which should be understood as the seven kinds of suffering.
The five kinds of causes termed "afflictive karma" are as previously explained: ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).

The seven kinds of fruits that arise are likewise as previously explained as the seven kinds of suffering, namely: consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Furthermore, these two types of emptiness regarding cause and effect are as follows:
within the cause there is no effect, and within the effect there is also no cause;
within the cause there is no cause, and within the effect there is also no effect.
The verse in the Sanskrit original concerning the wise one’s correspondence with emptiness is now rendered here as a single sentence:
"Regarding these two types of cause and effect thus described, if the cause is empty, the effect is also empty; if the effect is empty, the cause is also empty."
The cause is empty because it is empty; the fruit is empty because it is empty. One should accord with these four propositions.
Furthermore, there is further analysis:
"The four types of factors in the world exist through the conjunction of cause and effect."
The conjunction of afflictions, karma, and their fruits should be admitted as the six branches.

Regarding the existence [of phenomena] in the world through the conjunction of cause and fruit across four types of branches: the five kinds of causes and seven kinds of fruits taught for the three periods of time are, in brief, subsumed into four types, which sequentially constitute four divisions.
Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), as two dharmas of the past, constitute the first part;
consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*), belonging to the present time, constitute the second part.
Craving (tṛṣṇā), grasping (upādāna), and becoming (bhava) also constitute the third part in the present time;
birth (jāti) and old age and death (jarāmaraṇa) constitute the fourth part as two factors in the future time.
This refers to the fourfold division.

As for the allowance of six divisions consisting of afflictions, karma, and the fruits of bondage: when the three types—afflictions, karma, and retribution—are combined with the two roots of bondage, they constitute the six divisions.
Within this [twelvefold chain], from ignorance up to feeling, ignorance is the root; from craving up to old age and death, craving is the root.

Within the root of ignorance, ignorance itself is the affliction portion (*kleśa-bhāga*); volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the karma portion (*karma-bhāga*); and consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are the fruition portion (*vipāka-bhāga*).

Within the roots of craving (*tṛṣṇā-mūla*), craving and grasping (*upādāna*) belong to the category of afflictions (*kleśa*); existence (*bhava*) belongs to the category of karma; and birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) belong to the category of fruition (*vipāka*).
Furthermore, this is a concise summary of the divisions of the links (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Because they are subsumed within the link of existence, there are two sections and three summaries.
The causes and effects are combined into sections; the third and fourth sections are summarized and abbreviated.

Taking "existence" (bhava) as the fundamental section, two further sections are initiated: namely, the interval between existence and birth is the first section, and the interval between formations (saṃskāra) and consciousness (vijñāna) is the second section.
These two sections together constitute the section on karma and its fruit.
The third section consists of the intermingling of cause and effect within sensation (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
These three sections, in turn, are further condensed into four types of summaries.
Ignorance and volitional formations are the first summary.
Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are the second summary.
Craving, grasping, and existence—these three constitute the third summary.
Birth and old age and death—these two constitute the fourth summary.
These are called the three sections and the four summaries.
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions of stage and time within these dharmas:
two, three, two, three, and two. In the stage of suffering there are five dharmas:
the agent, the storehouse, the realm, the object, and the transformation of arising and circulation.
Regarding the factors: ignorance and formations are taught as two kinds;
consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases are taught as three kinds;
contact and feeling are taught as two kinds.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are said to be three kinds.
Furthermore, the two—birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—are said to be two kinds.

These five factors, within the state of suffering, should be understood according to their respective numbers as the agent, the womb, the objective field, the arising and turning, the birth, and the circulation therein.

Among these, ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are described as the agent within the state of suffering; consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are described as the embryo within the state of suffering; contact (*sparśa*) and sensation (*vedanā*) are described as the objective sphere within the state of suffering; craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are described as the activation and progression within the state of suffering; and birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are described as the circulation within the state of suffering.
Furthermore, regarding the distinctions among fruits:
the fruit of the arousal of delusion and the two fruits of retribution and outflow constitute the two [primary categories].
Within the divisions of the associated faculties, each one is further divided into three or two parts.

As previously stated, regarding these roots of ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), within the initial portion of the root of ignorance, there arises delusion that produces results and outflows; these are termed the four kinds of fruits.
The paths categorized into groups of one, three, and two should be understood as corresponding to their respective order.

Among these, ignorance is the fruit of delusion; volitional formations are the fruit of origination; consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases are the fruit of maturation; and contact and sensation are the fruit of outflow.
Furthermore, there are other residual fruits:
the fruit of affliction and deficiency, and the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) produced from transformation.
Within the various associated factors, there are two, one, one, and one dharma respectively.

As previously explained in the second section on the faculty of craving (*tṛṣṇendriya*), the results of burning affliction, deficiency, rebirth, and outflowing (*niṣyanda-phala*)—each according to its respective number—should be understood as corresponding to these factors herein.
Among these, craving and grasping are the result of affliction; becoming is the result of deficiency; birth is the result of emergence; and old age and death are the result of outflow.
Thus, there are eight results in all.
These consist of twelve kinds; because they are combined, they arise through conditions.
There is no sentient being and no life-force; they are empty and non-existent—this is known through wisdom.

Thus, beginning with ignorance (the ancient translation "ignorance" is correct; "lack of knowledge" is the proper term) and ending with old age and death, there are twelve links. Because their combination is preeminent, each arises through its respective condition.
Yet there are no sentient beings, no life-span, and no emptiness; this should be understood through wisdom.
Within this, there are no sentient beings because they are not solid.
There is no life-span because there is no self;
it is empty because there is no agent, for there is no agent.
There is no self and nothing belonging to a self; in the absence of self and within that which is without self—
The four kinds of ignorance are empty; the remaining factors are likewise so.
Ignorance is non-self.
Herein, ignorance is that which belongs to a non-self; because there is no self, within that which is non-self there is no ignorance.
Within the four kinds of ignorance and non-self, there is also no ignorance or emptiness.

Just as there is no ignorance or emptiness in the four kinds [of factors] in their respective order, so too should one know that the remaining members, such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and the rest, are all empty.
Free from the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism, this is precisely the Middle Way.
If awakening is fully accomplished, the essence of that awakening is the Buddhas.
"Existence" is the clinging to permanence; "non-existence" is the clinging to annihilation. These two extremes arise from this; they are produced by conditions.
Within those various states of existence, if one departs from these two extremes, one accords with the Middle Way.
If one does not understand this meaning, then the various non-Buddhists fall into the two extremes.
If one has awakened, then one is indeed all the Buddhas; as the Buddha is able to achieve [this] in the world, so it is for no other.
Having awakened, among the assembly, the Sage Seer taught non-self;
in the *Nagaropama-sūtra*, the Guide spoke this meaning.
Having awakened to this Middle Way therein, the Buddha declares among the assemblies: "There is no self and nothing belonging to a self.
You bhikṣus should know that those who cling to a self and what belongs to a self are merely foolish, childish, and ignorant worldlings of little learning.
Within conventional designations, there further arise the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self.
Monks, when [a person] arises, it is only suffering that arises; when they cease, it is only suffering that ceases.
This is as the meaning has already been explained by the Guide in the *Sūtra of the Simile of the City*.
Furthermore:
The *Kātyāyanāvavāda-sūtra* speaks of right view and the view of emptiness;
the *Prakaraṇapāda-sūtra* likewise speaks of the preeminent emptiness.
In these three sūtras and in other places, the Blessed One has extensively explained such characteristics as these:
"If one correctly understands dependent origination, one knows it to be associated with emptiness;
if one does not understand dependent origination, one will also not know that emptiness."
If there is correct knowledge regarding the dependent origination previously described, that knowledge is no different from this.
What, then, does it know?
It is said to know emptiness.

If one does not know dependent origination, one also does not know emptiness; that is, if one does not understand this dependent origination, it should be understood that one will likewise be unable to comprehend and enter into that emptiness.
If one gives rise to pride regarding emptiness, one will not feel weary of the aggregates;
if one holds the view of non-existence, one is deluded about the meaning of dependent origination.
If one gives rise to pride regarding emptiness, one does not feel weary; if one gives rise to pride in emptiness, one does not produce weariness and detachment toward the five aggregates.

If one possesses the view of non-existence and is thus deluded regarding the meaning of dependent origination, then because of this delusion concerning the meaning of dependent origination due to the view of non-existence, one will adopt whichever of the four views is taken: first, the view of annihilationism; second, the view of eternalism; third, the doctrine of creation by Īśvara; and fourth, the doctrine that all is produced by past karma.
Because they are not deluded regarding dependent origination, they abandon conceit and realize emptiness;
because they are weary of the aggregates, they are not deluded regarding karma and its fruit.

Regarding the line "Because they are not deluded regarding dependent origination, they abandon conceit and realize emptiness": if one is without a deluded mind concerning the various modes of dependent origination previously explained, and if one attains the abandonment of conceit regarding the grasping of a self and what belongs to a self, then one can enter into emptiness in accordance with the Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding "because one is weary of the aggregates, one is not deluded concerning karma and its results": because one grasps at a self and what belongs to a self within the five aggregates, one revolves incessantly throughout the world.
Because of weariness with those aggregates, one is neither inverted nor deluded regarding the continuity of karma and its results.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of this?
Karma acts as a condition for rebirth, yet it is not without depending upon this [continuity].
"Empty conditions must exist; they are the requisites for the experience of karmic retribution.

Karma acts as a condition for the continuity of birth, nor is it the case that there is no such condition. Regarding the afflictions and karmic retribution as previously explained, sentient beings are impelled by such wholesome and unwholesome karma to arise in a continuous succession across the horizontal, vertical, and upward directions; were it not for this karma, it would not act as a condition.
If it were otherwise, one would not experience the retribution for actions performed, or one would lose what has already been performed.

If there were such a recipient of the karmic retribution of emptiness as its condition, then although there is the experiencing of retribution from these wholesome and unwholesome karmas, their intrinsic nature is empty and originally lacks a self; one should likewise know that the arising of those conditions is also of an empty nature.
That meaning shall now be explained further in brief.
Regarding the distinctions among the twelve links, which were previously described as dependent origination,
those afflictions, karmas, and sufferings are subsumed according to their respective natures within these three categories.
Beginning with ignorance and ending with old age and death, these are the specific divisions of dependent origination as previously explained.
Among them, three are afflictions, two are karma, and seven are suffering; all are thus subsumed.
From three arise two; from two arise seven;
from seven again arise three. Thus does the wheel of existence revolve.

From the three factors of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) arise the two factors of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*). From those two arise the seven branches: consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Within those seven branches, as previously explained, three types are produced again; from those three, two are further produced, and then again seven.
Thus, these two types continue in succession without interruption, and in this manner the wheel of existence revolves.
Causes and effects give rise to the various worlds; there are no separate sentient beings.
It is only within empty phenomena that empty phenomena themselves arise. Regarding "causes and effects give rise to the various worlds;

there are no separate sentient beings": ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are the five named causes. Consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are the seven named effects.

One should understand that all these pervasive worldly designations—whether as a self, a sentient being, a life-span, a living creature, a person, a human, or an agent—are merely false conceptual constructions.
How does that arise?

It is simply that from empty phenomena, empty phenomena themselves arise. That is to say, within the emptiness of intrinsic nature, afflictions, karma, and its fruits are merely conventional designations; it is only these phenomena of empty, conventional designations—afflictions, karma, and their fruits—that arise. This is the meaning.
Dependent on conditions, afflictions arise; dependent on conditions, karma also arises;
and dependent on conditions, retribution also arises. There is not a single thing that does not have conditions.

If there are afflictions, then there are various and immeasurable karmas, as well as the various fruits of retribution produced by those karmas; all of these are due to common conditions. One should know that there is not a single dharma that exists without causes and conditions.
Furthermore, to clarify that meaning, another analogy is now set forth:
Recitation, lamps, seals, mirrors, and sound; Sunlight, seeds, and vinegar— In these various continuities there is no transmigration;
The wise should contemplate these two [cases].

As in the case of recitation, there is the one who instructs the recitation and the one who receives the recitation; yet, the instruction of the recitation does not transfer to the recipient of the recitation. For what reason? Because the instructor of the recitation remains established, and because they remain established, that instruction of the recitation does not continue [into the other].
Why is this? Because it is neither self-originated nor unoriginated.
Just as a lamp arises in succession, it is not the case that the initial lamp transmigrates, nor is it the case that the second lamp arises without a cause.

In this way, there are two kinds: the seal and its image; two kinds: the face and the mirror; two kinds: the sound and the echo; two kinds: the sun and the fire; two kinds: the seed and the sprout; and two kinds: the sour taste and the salivation of the tongue.
Both of these types [of continuity] are entirely non-transmigrating, yet they are not unarisen, nor do they arise without cause.
These two types of five-aggregate continuity proceed in succession; it is not that the first aggregate transmigrates, yet the second aggregate is neither unarisen nor does it arise without cause.
The wise person should correctly contemplate this continuity of the aggregates (*skandha-santāna*) as it proceeds without shifting from its sequence.
Furthermore, there are ten types of internal-external correspondences that should all be known.

Regarding the ten aspects within and without: first, because it is impermanent; second, because it is not annihilated; third, because it does not transmigrate; fourth, because cause and effect are linked without an interval; fifth, because it is not that [external] entity; sixth, because it is not something distinct; seventh, because there is no agent; eighth, because it is not without cause; ninth, because it perishes moment by moment; and tenth, because it is linked with its own kind of fruit.

Because all external seeds have been extinguished without remainder; because the sprout does not arise from what is permanent; because the sprout arises now where it was previously non-existent after the seeds have been extinguished without remainder; because there is no transmigration, yet the continuity of that which is characterized [by the seed] is without interruption as cause and effect succeed one another; because there is no distinction between the intermediate seed and the sprout; because its essence does not arise from itself; because it does not arise from the conjunction of separate causes and conditions; because there is no agent, with the seed serving as the cause; because it is not without cause, for the seed, sprout, stalk, branch, leaf, flower, and fruit arise in succession from one another; and because, in momentary destruction, the sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent fruits emerge according to the distinctions of their respective causes.

Regarding the mutual connection of similar fruits (*sabhāga-phala*): among these, the first ten points are as follows. First, because the aggregates at the moment of death (*cyuti-skandha*) perish without remainder, they are impermanent (*anitya*).
Second, because the aggregates of the subsequent birth-moment (*upapatti-skandha*) are obtained, there is no annihilation (*uccheda*).

Third, once the aggregates at the moment of death have perished without remainder, the aggregates of the subsequent birth-moment arise where they previously did not exist; therefore, there is no transmigration (*saṃkrānti*).
Fourth, because the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha*) is without interruption and cause and effect follow one another, there is no interval between them;
fifth, because there is a distinction between the aggregates at the limit of death and those of the subsequent birth-moment, they do not possess the same substance;
sixth, because they arise from that [previous state], they are not something entirely different.
Seventh, because of the harmony of causes and conditions, there is no creator;
eighth, because afflictions and karma serve as causes, it is not without cause;
ninth, because the stages of kalala, arbuda, peśī, ghana, āṃsaka, birth from the womb, infancy, childhood, youth, and adulthood arise one after another, they perish moment by moment.
Tenth is the perfuming by the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Because the fruit arises and evolves in accordance with the distinctions of its causes, it is bound to its corresponding fruit.
Furthermore, there are three verses:
Just as the flame of a lamp arises in succession, so too is the aggregate of consciousness;
there is no accumulation from the prior limit to the subsequent limit.
Though unarisen, it appears to arise; it is subject to destruction and lacks any inherent cohesion.
That which is produced likewise has no abiding, yet this activity proceeds.
If one can perceive that what arises from those conditions is empty,
and if one understands those designations, then one accords with the Middle Way.

Among these, ignorance, volitional formations, craving, clinging, and becoming constitute the Truth of Origination; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death constitute the Truth of Suffering.

Regarding those twelve links, the Truth of the Path is the means for realizing their cessation; that is to say, the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path are called the Truth of the Path.
